staged_source_snapshot.description: Stage 01 reproduced against this preserved vulnerable checkout. Its line map matches the saved AddressSanitizer frame at `mrbgems/mruby-sprintf/src/sprintf.c:841` and the staged patch hunk in `get_num()`.

classification.classification_note: The saved AddressSanitizer report aborts in `__asan_memcpy` because `mrb_str_format()` passes a negative length to `PUSH`, whose macro expansion performs `memcpy(&buf[blen], s, l)`.

bug_description.original: mrb_str_format in mrbgems/mruby-sprintf/src/sprintf.c computes an incorrect (overflowed/negative) length when parsing numeric format specifiers, which can cause memcpy to be called with a negative size (ASAN "negative-size-param"). This leads to crashes and can result in out‑of‑bounds heap memory access or corruption, potentially enabling exploitation.
bug_description.normalized: The staged witness is the exact text file `% %.4294629629s %%  `. `mruby` admits it as Ruby source, executes code that reaches `mrb_f_sprintf()`, and hands the format string into `mrb_str_format()`. While parsing the `%.4294629629s` precision, `get_num()` accumulates decimal digits into 64-bit `mrb_int next_n` and accepts `4294629629` because it only checks `mrb_int` overflow. Vulnerable `get_num()` then narrows that value directly into 32-bit `int prec` with `*valp = (int)next_n`, producing `prec == -337667` for this witness instead of rejecting the oversized precision. The `%s` formatter treats that negative precision as `prec < slen`, moves a temporary pointer backward from the string base, and copies the negative value into both `slen` and `len`. No width branch is active, so execution falls through to `PUSH(RSTRING_PTR(str), len)`. `CHECK(len)` does not reject negative sizes because its loop only runs for `l >= bsiz - blen`, and the macro expansion then calls `memcpy(&buf[blen], s, l)` with negative `l`, producing the saved AddressSanitizer `negative-size-param` crash at `sprintf.c:841`.

source.description: Source. While parsing the attacker-controlled `%.4294629629s` field, `mrb_str_format()` invokes `get_num()` on the decimal precision digits so they become vulnerability-relevant numeric state in `prec`.
source.value_from: The staged `poc` bytes are exactly `b'% %.4294629629s %%  '`. `mrb_load_detect_file_cxt()` admits that file as Ruby source, execution reaches `mrb_f_sprintf()`, and `argv[0]` is passed as `fmt` to `mrb_str_format()` at `sprintf.c:566`. When control reaches this statement, `p` points at the digits after `.` in the `%s` conversion, so `GETNUM` consumes the attacker-chosen decimal string `4294629629`.

sink.description: AddressSanitizer crash site. `mrb_str_format()` passes the negative `len` derived from the malformed precision into `PUSH`, whose macro expansion reaches `memcpy(&buf[blen], s, l)` with `l < 0` and triggers the saved `negative-size-param` abort.

root_cause.description: Root cause fixed by the patch. `get_num()` narrows the parsed decimal value from `mrb_int next_n` into 32-bit `int` without first checking whether it fits in `INT_MAX`, so oversized numeric format specifiers become negative `prec`/`width` values instead of being rejected.

tainted_value_origin.description: Ruby execution turns the witness into a `sprintf` call and passes the attacker-controlled format object as `fmt` into `mrb_str_format()`, where the decimal precision digits are later parsed into `prec`.
tainted_value_origin.value_from: The saved crash stack is `mrb_str_format -> mrb_f_sprintf -> mrb_vm_exec`, so the witness reaches this call site before the vulnerable precision parser runs.

parser_admitted.description: Sample-specific source-format gate. The witness does not begin with the `RITE` bytecode header, so this predicate selects the Ruby-source parser path instead of the binary `.mrb` loader.

admitted_location.code: return mrb_load_exec(mrb, mrb_parse_file_continue(mrb, fp, leading.b, bufsize, c), c);

coarse_trace.summary: The staged file is admitted as Ruby source rather than `.mrb` bytecode, and VM execution later reaches `mrb_f_sprintf()`.

While parsing `%.4294629629s`, `get_num()` accepts the decimal precision in 64-bit `mrb_int` and then truncates it into negative 32-bit `int prec` because the vulnerable code lacks the `INT_MAX` range check added by the patch.
The `%s` formatter treats that negative precision as a truncation bound, copies it into negative `slen` and `len`, and bypasses the width-handling branch because the witness specified no width.
The final `PUSH(RSTRING_PTR(str), len)` call reaches the macro expansion with negative `len`; `CHECK` does not reject it, and `memcpy` aborts with the saved AddressSanitizer `negative-size-param`.

fine_trace.note: Source. In the `case '.'` precision parser, `mrb_str_format()` calls `get_num()` on the attacker-controlled digit run after `.` in `%.4294629629s`, materializing that decimal text as numeric precision state.
The digit loop consumes `4294629629` into `mrb_int next_n`. On this build `mrb_int` is wide enough that neither overflow check fires, so `next_n` ends the loop as the positive value `4294629629`.

Root cause. Vulnerable `get_num()` narrows `next_n == 4294629629` directly into 32-bit `int`, so the parsed precision becomes `-337667` for this witness. The staged patch inserts `if (next_n > INT_MAX || next_n < 0) return NULL;` immediately before this cast to block exactly this transition.
The `%s` formatter reaches its precision-truncation branch because `FPREC` is set for `%.4294629629s` and the narrowed `prec` is negative while `slen = RSTRING_LEN(str)` is non-negative.

Inside that branch, the negative precision is propagated into the derived copy state: the temporary pointer moves backward from the string base, `slen` is overwritten with the same negative value, and `len` becomes the same negative offset that will later be used as the copy length.

The width-handling branch is not taken on this witness because the malformed specifier provided precision but no width, so `FWIDTH` is clear and execution falls through toward the unconditional final `PUSH` at line 841.

fine_trace.code:
#define CHECK(l) do {                           \
  while ((l) >= bsiz - blen) {\
    if (bsiz > MRB_INT_MAX/2) mrb_raise(mrb, E_ARGUMENT_ERROR, "too big specifier"); \
    bsiz*=2;\
  }\
  mrb_str_resize(mrb, result, bsiz);\
  buf = RSTRING_PTR(result);\
} while (0)
fine_trace.note: The size check that `PUSH` uses does not reject negative lengths. With `l == len == -337667`, the loop condition `l >= bsiz - blen` is false immediately, so the macro preserves the destination buffer state and allows the negative size to propagate to the copy primitive.

Sink. The call site recorded in the saved AddressSanitizer trace passes `len < 0` into `PUSH`; its macro expansion executes `memcpy(&buf[blen], s, l)` with that negative `l`, and ASan aborts with `negative-size-param` at `sprintf.c:841`.

format.contract: The verified trigger is the exact witness text `% %.4294629629s %%  `. Its load-bearing property is the `%s` conversion with precision digits `4294629629` and no width field: vulnerable `get_num()` accepts that decimal as `mrb_int`, truncates it to 32-bit `int prec == -337667`, and the `%s` path later reuses that negative precision as copy length `len`.
